extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers and essayists / creative writers interested in moral storytelling, characterization, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and principles for composing moralizing narratives and character sketches: how to show vice and virtue, satisfy readers' sense of justice, use distinctive mannerisms to reveal character, structure expository essays, and manage tone (cheerfulness vs. austerity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers' love of justice; punishment of villain as satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mind of Man is naturally a Lover of Justice, and when we read a Story wherein a Criminal is overtaken, in whom there is no Quality which is the Object of Pity, the Soul enjoys a certain Revenge for the Offence done to its Nature, in the wicked Actions committed in the preceding Part of the History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives that show a villain's wicked actions and then depict the criminal being overtaken or punished provide emotional closure and satisfy the reader's sense of justice. Example in text: Rhynsault's crimes are narrated and he is ultimately executed by the Duke. Anti-pattern: leaving a clearly vicious character unpunished or unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vice and motive through actions rather than abstract labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict characters' dispositions and inclinations (e.g., 'a Man of a warm Constitution, and violent Inclination to Women') through the concrete acts they commit—their deceit, manipulation and violations—so readers infer moral qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete narrative incidents (imprisoning a husband under false pretence, demanding sexual compliance for a pardon, ordering an execution) to make vice intelligible and believable. The narrator's prefatory claim that the reader will understand better from the narration than from an introduction encourages 'show, don't tell.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by distinctive physical mannerisms and small gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal social types and individual character by specific, repeated physical actions and postures (e.g., Glycera's dancing walk, Chloe's familiar run, Dulcissa's pretty shiver, carrying fans between hands, sitting with hoop'd petticoats falling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create memorable characters by cataloguing small, observable behaviours and mannerisms that signal disposition and strategy (coquetry, indolence, artifice). Examples: Dulceorella's staring technique, the 'Swingers' who shout and shriek while being swung. Anti-pattern: vague or generic descriptions that fail to distinguish one character from another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and content to audience tastes; entertainment often trumps homily
rubrics_metrics.description: A loose trivial Song gains the Affections, when a wise Homily is not attended to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming to be noticed or persuasive, recognize that light, appealing entertainment often attracts readers more readily than moral instruction. Writers who insist only on didacticism risk being ignored; consider balancing instruction with agreeable forms (song, lively anecdote) to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose recommendation (introductory) letters with modesty, reasons, and service to recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: In recommending someone, exhibit 'a Slowness to ask a Favour, a strong Reason for being unable to deny his good Word any longer, and that it is a Service to the Person to whom he recommends, to comply with what is asked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good letters of introduction should avoid presumptuousness, provide a clear motive for the request, and frame the recommendation as beneficial to the addressee. The translated epistle from Horace models the courteous structure and necessary circumstances for a recommendatory letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor honesty in recommendations to recipient's needs (include relevant faults)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honest, candid recommendations that mention relevant traits—even faults—can be more useful: e.g., Jack Toper recommends Thomas by noting he was 'turned away because he was too good for me' and describing habits that fit the prospective employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the recommended person's qualities (and drawbacks) to the recipient's expectations and circumstances; a truthful portrait helps both parties. Anti-pattern: passing on 'a worthless Creature' through flattery or omission of important character traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance cheerfulness and seriousness in moral or religious writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion and virtue should not extinguish cheerfulness: 'The true Spirit of Religion cheers, as well as composes the Soul; it banishes indeed all Levity of Behaviour... but in exchange fills the Mind with a perpetual Serenity, uninterrupted Chearfulness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid representing religion (or moral seriousness) as perpetual melancholy; employ a tone that contains serenity and good-humour to invite readers rather than repel them. Anti-pattern: portraying piety as unsociable gloom that discourages engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize exposition into clear views and account for causes and purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid common beaten tracks of observation, consider a subject in several distinct views (e.g., number, dispersion, adherence) and then examine natural and providential reasons for those particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure essays by enumerating perspectives, then systematically analyze causes (natural/social) and higher-order reasons (providential, rhetorical) as applicable. Example: the essay on the Jews divides the topic into three views and then assigns natural and providential explanations for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain congruence between character's stage of life and behavior; avoid ridicule from inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients allotted inclinations and objects of desire to every stage of life; when the order is inverted (e.g., feeble old men attempting the pomp of youth) the dignity of human nature is violated and becomes ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or depicting characters, ensure age-appropriate manners, attire, and pursuits. Anti-pattern: an old man dressing and living with the splendor and indulgence of youth, producing grotesque or comic effects and undermining credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use story examples rather than abstract introduction to illustrate principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle is often better understood 'from the following Narration itself, than from any thing which I can say to introduce it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To teach or persuade, prefer concrete narrative illustration over abstract exposition: let a well-chosen tale demonstrate the moral or point you wish readers to grasp. Example: the prefatory remark leads into the Rhynsault story to exemplify the claim about love of justice.
